doc.title: Bobby Watson interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, January 19, 1996

title: Music as a language; Herb Jeffries and Sidney Bechet
summary: He calls music a language, recounts Herb Jeffries' Bechet stories from the Rainbow Room gig, and says the instrument is his barometer and he urges students to say something.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Let me ask you one other thing, is you know we talked to a lot of jazz artists and in their own ways, in their own words they, many of them confirm that there is a type of spirituality in this music. In other words the music is more than just the technical ability to move fast over the keys.

Yeah. It’s, I believe that it’s a language and that the notes and all the things you learn, the exercises, the calisthenics, over the years are basically just the framework of the language, and once you learn how to manipulate that, like the alphabet and sentence structure, and that’s comparable in music as the different modes and all the intervals, which are the building blocks of the music, that’s what you’re able to pick. You know if you do a rising line, that brings a certain feeling or if you drop your line that gives a certain feeling of melancholy. So I believe that it’s a language and I know that Herb Jeffries, I had a chance to work with him when I was working with Panama Francis up in the Rainbow Room. And Herb Jeffries came in for a month from Paris. And he told me a lot of stories because he knew Sidney Bechet. So I figured I’d get pretty close-hand information about the history of the music. And he says that during the jam sessions, Sidney Bechet would be playing and he would say, “Now I’m going to call my dog.” And he’d play something, I don’t know what it was, a sound, and his dog would come in. And I think it relates to when they took the drums away when we arrived in America, that the whole language of the drums, because you know the drums were used for © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

communication. So I believe that that sublimated into the instruments and so this communication is sort of the underlying thing about the instruments. Because I know I feel there is something that you know when I’m blowing, I get something off your chest, you know when you’re playing, that you really can’t put into words. But when you’re playing an instrument, after you’re done you feel satisfied like if you said something you needed to say that day you know? And I know depending on how I feel, my instrument lets me know what kind of day it’s going to be. That’s for sure. I mean that’s my barometer. When I pick that horn up I know if it’s going to be a good day or how well I’m feeling or how rested I am or how tired I am. And I think that’s the thing that I try to get over to the students you know, is you learn this, now what do you want to say? What do you want to play? See the whole fun thing about jazz was you know you’re not supposed to do what’s there. I’m going to read the part but after I got the part I’m going to start adding notes and changing it, and I’m going to take it the way I hear it. You know? And so it’s like man, you know, why do you want to play something the same way this guy did it? Simple things like this you know. Or I used to sit in front of the T.V. and I would memorize or play along with the theme songs on T.V. Just use your ear. Things like this are certain things that guide you in this music.
